tagline.text: Iloilo's little Baguio, spent in a misty pine forest

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–3,000 per person (based on a 2-day, 1-night camping trip)

children.text: A pine plantation spread across the Bucari highland in Leon, about 2 hours northwest of Iloilo City, known as "Iloilo's little Baguio." Enjoy camping and a walk to the Mansiga viewpoint in the cool air, and combine it with terraced vegetable fields and Imoy Falls.
Bucari is a highland village in the mountains of central Panay Island, about
20km
up a mountain road west of Leon town proper and about
60km
from Iloilo City. The Tabiauan area, where the campground sits, is around

above sea level, with surrounding peaks rising much higher, so temperatures run about 5–10 degrees cooler than the lowlands even at midday. This cool climate and the pine forest have earned Leon the nickname "Iloilo's Summer Capital," and Bucari, "Iloilo's little Baguio."

The pines here aren't a natural forest but a plantation the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) planted decades ago to restore the Aganan River watershed. The Tabiauan plantation area covers about 5,000 hectares, and tourism materials describe it as the only pine plantation in West Visayas. Locals commonly call it Benguet pine, though some sources list a different species. Since
, a new reforestation project involving private companies, the DENR, and the Leon municipal government has been underway, planting about 340,000 seedlings across roughly 225 hectares.

Visitors mainly head to the roughly 1.5-hectare Bucari campground and the Mansiga viewpoint, reached by climbing a stairway lined with the 14 Stations of the Cross. On a clear day, the viewpoint looks out over pine ridges and terraced vegetable plots all the way to the plains toward Iloilo City. Nearby barangays scatter valley waterfalls like Imoy Falls and Catao Falls among rice paddies and vegetable terraces, letting you combine forest and water play in a single day.

This isn't a resort-style attraction but a public campground in a mountain village, so facilities are basic and parts of the road are still rough. In exchange, fireflies and stars appear at night, and mist blankets the forest in the morning. It suits Iloilo locals craving cool air instead of air conditioning, campers wanting to pitch a tent for a night, and travelers who've toured Iloilo City and Miagao and want a change of scenery in the mountains.

blocks.title: A Night at the Pine Campground

children.text: The campground at Tabiauan, where you can pitch a tent beneath tall pines, is the heart of Bucari. Nights drop to around
, perfect for a campfire and long sleeves, and on clear nights you can see fireflies and stars.
A roughly
30–45 minute

climb up a stairway lined with the 14 Stations of the Cross and a forest trail brings you to a viewpoint on a rocky ridge. It's Bucari's best vantage point, taking in the pine forest, terraced fields, and layers of mountain ridges at once.
A pine tree that survived Typhoon Frank in
while leaning has become a famous photo spot, its trunk stretching out toward the cliff. The edge is steep, so stay behind the safety line.

Imoy Falls, in a valley in Barangay Camandag, has a swimming pool at its base — a great way to cool off after hiking. A larger waterfall continues upstream, and the flow peaks toward the end of the rainy season.

blocks.title: Catao Falls and a Valley Walk

children.text: Several small waterfalls, including Catao Falls, dot the area around Bucari. Many trails aren't marked, so it's best to ask a village guide or habal-habal driver to lead the way.

Leon is known as "Iloilo's vegetable basket," growing plenty of cabbage, carrots, string beans, and chayote. The terraced fields and rice paddies carved into the hillsides are most beautiful when the morning sun hits them.

blocks.title: A Morning Walk Through the Misty Forest

children.text: Mist drifting through the pines at sunrise is Bucari's signature scene. Take a slow walk along the forest trails around the campground between
6 and 8am

Roadside stalls at the campground entrance and along the way sell freshly picked tomatoes, cucumbers, and pomelo at low prices. Picking up a bag on the way back is one of the small pleasures of a Bucari trip.

If you're doing a day trip by public transport, you need to leave early in the morning. Jeepneys coming down from Bucari often stop running in the early afternoon, so ask the driver about the return schedule as soon as you arrive.

From Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO) takes about
1 hour 10 minutes
, with direct flights also available from Cebu, Davao, and Clark. Cabatuan, where the airport sits, is fairly close to Leon, so renting a car gets you from the airport to Bucari in about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
If traveling by public transport, it's easier to take an airport shuttle van or taxi into Iloilo City and catch a Leon-bound jeepney from the Jaro terminal.
Leon-bound jeepneys run frequently from the Jaro Big Market terminal in Iloilo City (also boardable in front of Robinsons Pavia). It takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
, for around
one-way.

45 minutes–1 hour

one-way, generally departing once full from around
7am
until about
2–3pm

2–3pm

7–8am
Chartering a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) from Leon plaza to the campground takes about
35–45 minutes
, for around
one-way. Negotiate the fare with the driver in advance if you want them to wait and take you to the waterfalls too.
From Iloilo City via Leon is about
60km
, taking
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
. The road climbing from Leon Poblacion up to Bucari is being paved with concrete, but some stretches remain steep and rough, so an SUV or pickup is safer than a regular car.
A rental car or a driver-included van charter runs about
per day, saving a group significant time compared to public transport. Don't push it on the dirt sections after heavy rain, as they get slippery.
The best time to visit Bucari is the dry season,
December–May
December–February
in particular brings a northeast wind that keeps daytime temperatures around
, with some early mornings dropping to around
, so a heavy jacket is worth packing. This is the best window for catching morning mist, fireflies, and clear views all at once.
March–May
is midsummer, when the lowlands climb to
, so Iloilo locals flock to the "summer capital" of Bucari to escape the heat. The campground and cottages fill up fast during Holy Week and
April–May
weekends, so check with the municipal tourism office in advance.
June–November

is the rainy season, with afternoon showers and thick fog rolling in daily, making dirt paths and stairs very slippery. Waterfalls carry the most water during this period, but stream levels can rise suddenly. During
August–November
, when typhoons cross the Visayas, landslides and washed-out roads are a risk, so be sure to check weather forecasts and municipal advisories.

The most common way to stay in Bucari is pitching a tent at the campground. You can bring your own tent or rent one from the caretaker, and there are restrooms and basic washing facilities. Groups can rent the campground's cottages, greenhouses, and guesthouses (about

a night for 4–8 people), though there are few of these and they fill up early on weekends. Pine Ridge Bucari Mountain Resort, in nearby Barangay Bacolod, has dormitory-style rooms and a restaurant. A Bucari Pavilion with dormitory-style lodging at Tabiauan, supported by a tourism department agency, is also planned, so check the Leon municipal tourism office's Facebook page for whether it's operating and its rates.

The sari-sari stores and stalls inside the campground sell only cup noodles, drinks, and simple rice meals. For a proper meal, arrange it with the caretaker in advance or buy groceries in Iloilo City and cook them yourself. Local dishes worth trying include Ilonggo-style linactang — native chicken grilled over charcoal, then simmered in a broth with garlic, onion, and tomato — native chicken adobo, and dishes made with vegetables fresh from the Bucari fields. Leon town has a growing number of vegetable farms, strawberry farms, and cafes worth stopping at along the way.
Bucari is much colder than the lowlands. If you're camping, be sure to bring long sleeves, a light down jacket or fleece, and a sleeping bag or blanket.
There are no ATMs at the campground or in the village. Bring cash for entrance fees, transport, and food from Iloilo City or Leon town.
Cell signal is weak or absent in many spots. Settle your return transport and communication plans before heading up the mountain.
The Mansiga viewpoint stairs and the trail to the waterfalls turn to mud after rain. Sturdy-soled sneakers or trekking sandals are best.
If you're camping or visiting as a group, notifying the Leon municipal tourism information center in advance makes cottage booking and local guidance easier.
The best light for photos is early morning as the mist starts to clear and late afternoon when the sun is low and soft.
Bring plenty of food and water, but carry all your trash back out. The campground sits inside a protected plantation.
If combining this with Iloilo City sightseeing or Miagao Church, it's efficient to spend a night in Bucari and head down to the southern coast the next day.

The mountain road up to Bucari gets slippery after rain, with some stretches narrow and steep. Landslides or road closures are possible during the rainy and typhoon seasons, so check the latest notices from the Leon municipal government, and avoid driving the mountain road after dark.
The area around Mansiga viewpoint and the leaning pine is a cliff edge. Don't lean out too far for photos, and keep a close eye on children.
The waterfall pools are hard to judge for depth and the rocks are slippery. Water levels can rise suddenly after rain, so avoid swimming then.
The pine forest is prone to fire during the dry season. Build campfires and cook only in designated areas, and never discard cigarette butts.
Environmental fees, entrance fees, cottage rates, and jeepney schedules change often. Check the municipal tourism office's notices before you go.
The surrounding vegetable and strawberry farms are mostly private property. Ask the owner's permission before entering or taking photos.
